record.paper_title: Achievement sets – current results and open problems
record.original_question: Given any achievable Cantor set C, must there exist achievable Cantorvals D′ and D′′ such that C + D′ is a Cantorval while C + D′′ is an interval?

evidence.quote: Does there exist, for any achievable Cantor set C, achievable Cantorvals D′ and D′′ such that C + D′ is a Cantorval and C + D′′ is an interval?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. For a sequence $(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of positive real numbers with $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n < \infty$, the achievement set (or set of subsums) of $(a_n)$ is
$$E(a_n) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{n\in A} a_n : A \subseteq \mathbb{N} \,\Bigr\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}.$$
A classical theorem (Guthrie–Nymann) states that for every absolutely convergent series of positive terms, $E(a_n)$ is exactly one of the following:
(i) a finite set, (ii) a finite union of nondegenerate closed intervals, (iii) a (topological) Cantor set, i.e. a nonempty compact set with no isolated points and empty interior, or (iv) a Cantorval, i.e. a nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$ which is the closure of its interior, has uncountably many connected components, and such that both endpoints of every nondegenerate component are accumulation points of degenerate (one-point) components.

A subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is called achievable if $S = E(a_n)$ for some absolutely convergent series of positive reals; one then speaks of an achievable Cantor set, an achievable Cantorval, etc. For $A,B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, the algebraic sum is
$$A + B \;=\; \{\, a + b : a \in A,\, b \in B \,\}.$$

Question. Is it true that for every achievable Cantor set $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ there exist achievable Cantorvals $D'$ and $D''$ such that $C + D'$ is a Cantorval and $C + D''$ is a nondegenerate closed interval?
